idiom_name: public static operators per type plus C# 11 operator interfaces (IComparisonOperators / IEqualityOperators) and record synthesis
implementation_notes: Operators exist, but only as public static members declared in the type itself and pairwise (== with !=, < with >, <= with >=), so every member of a family needs its operator set written by hand - there is no CRTP and operators are not inherited. The family-wide equivalent is generic code constrained by the operator interfaces of the generic-math feature (IEqualityOperators<T, T, bool>, IComparisonOperators<T, T, bool>, INumber<T>); C# 11 static abstract/static virtual interface members can even carry a default operator body, but that default is reachable only through the constrained type parameter, so the implementing type still declares or explicitly implements its operators. Records synthesise Equals/GetHashCode/==/!= for the value-semantics half and IComparable<T> provides the ordering consumed by the BCL, so hand-written operators are worth it mainly for numeric or money-like types where operator syntax is the point.
pitfalls: Interface default operators are not inherited by the implementing type - they are usable only through a constrained type parameter - so implementing an auto-comparison interface does not remove the per-type boilerplate.
== and != must be overloaded together, and an overloaded == should come with Equals/GetHashCode; a record already synthesises that pair, so overriding one half by hand silently splits the contract.
Generic-math constraints are viral and heavy: every caller repeats the constraint, and user types must implement a wide interface surface to qualify - rarely worth it outside numeric abstractions.
